domain: Religious Studies / Rabbinic Judaism / Commitment System Theory
topic_summary: Analysis of rabbinic preservation of Temple sacrifice law (Kodashim) across 1,900 years without performance. The kernel contest: study-as-exercise reading treats the kernel as occupied through continuous engagement; performance-only reading treats it as archived husk awaiting messianic restoration. This collapses the boundary between exercising a commitment and archiving its symbol—a D1/D4 boundary case in commitment system theory.

key_entities: Seder Kodashim (fifth order of Mishnah, 11 tractates on Temple sacrifice)
Rabbinic Judaism post-70 CE (interpretive authority after Temple destruction)
Jacob Neusner (20th c., 'map without territory' interpretation)
Temple Mount Institute / Modern Yeshivot (contemporary messianic-preparation institutions)
Palestinian/Babylonian Talmud (differential treatment: no Palestinian Talmud on Kodashim, abbreviated Babylonian)
key_tensions: Study vs Performance: Is engagement with Kodashim itself the fulfillment or merely preparation for future restoration?
Kernel vs Husk: Does continuous study occupy the commitment or merely archive its symbol?
Historical Neglect vs Theological Necessity: Maimonides' era saw widespread neglect justified by 'no practical benefit,' contradicting study-as-sacred-exercise position
key_mechanisms: Mishnaic Codification (200 CE): Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi's redaction stabilized oral traditions as written kernel
Study-as-Substitute Doctrine: Maimonides' ruling that studying sacrifice law equals performing it
key_absences: No Palestinian Talmud on Kodashim (suggests limited practical engagement in Land of Israel)
Centuries of documented neglect (contradicts continuous-occupation claim)

axiom_contradictions.basis: Study-as-exercise holds that intellectual engagement IS the complete fulfillment of the mitzvah (no future performance needed). Performance-only holds that study is preparation for future physical restoration (current engagement is incomplete). No single framework can hold both: either study completes the obligation or it does not.

Study-as-exercise holds the kernel is occupied (sacrifice law remains living divine command). Substitution-archive holds the kernel was superseded (sacrifice replaced by prayer/study, now archived as memorial). No single framework can hold both: either the original commandment persists or it was replaced.

omegas.description: Does the D1/D4 boundary (kernel occupied vs husk archived) collapse into a false dichotomy? All three readings may coexist as licensed plurality within rabbinic Judaism—different communities instantiate different readings without requiring global resolution. The 'contest' may be a feature, not a bug.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel recognition; axiom contradictions declared but readings coexist historically

omegas.description: Does historical neglect (no Palestinian Talmud, Maimonides-era abandonment) falsify the study-as-exercise reading, or does it merely show that reading was contested rather than universal? Neglect may indicate performance_only was dominant, not that study-as-exercise was incoherent.
omegas.source: Deferred axis talmudic_neglect_pattern; tension between theological necessity and historical practice

omegas.description: Is performance_only's high extractiveness score correct, or does it reverse victim/beneficiary? If messianic preparation is sincere (not cynical), the 'victim' (those treating archive as living practice) may be the extractive party—demanding immediate fulfillment from a commitment explicitly deferred to messianic age.
omegas.source: §2 epsilon_bin classification for performance_only reading; beneficiary/victim assignment contested

omegas.description: Does Neusner's 'map without territory' interpretation (substitution_archive reading) commit epistemic trespass? His framework may impose secular academic categories ('fictitious territory') onto a system that rejects the map/territory distinction—for Maimonides, the map IS the territory.
omegas.source: F34 epistemic trespass check; Neusner's interpretive authority over internal rabbinic theology contested
